Accused
Judgment:
1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules.

The
acc
used is stated to be the vendor cum proprietor of M/s National Bakery from where the food article, that is, 'Vegetable Sauce' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 24.06.2009, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Suniti Kumar Gupta and Field Assistant (FA) Ashok Kumar under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh.M.S.Vats reached along with their staff at the handcart of M/s. National Bakery, at the corner of Allahabad Bank, Parliament Street, Connaught Place, New Delhi-110001,
where the accused was found conducting the business and having stored for sale various food articles.

The food officials lifted a sample of Vegetable Sauce, as lying in sealed glass bottles of 500 gm each, bearing no label declaration, from the vendor accused as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama,
etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report dated 13.07.2009, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the grounds In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
1

that it was coloured with synthetic colouring matters 'Tartrazine', 'Sunset Yellow FCF' and 'Ponceu 4 R', that it contained saccharine (artificial sweetner), that the Total Soluble Solids and Acidity contents were less than the prescribed minimum limits, and also that the sample was misbranded because of complete violation of Rule 32 of PFA Rules.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 11.02.2010 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of PFA Act read with Rules 23 and 29 of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act, as well as violation of Section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act read with Rules 24, 47 and 32 of PFA Rules, as punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 11.02.2010.

The accused appeared but never filed any application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from the Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
4.
The matter was then listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI Suniti Kumar Gupta and PW-2 FI N.N.Sharma.

On the basis of their depositions, charge was framed against the accused on 03.07.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A)
PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b),
(j) and (m) of PFA Act, as well as violation of Section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

At the trial, the witnesses examined in pre-charge stage of evidence were recalled for cross-examination in post-charge stage and additionally, prosecution examined PW-3 Sh. M.S.Vats and PW-4 FA Ashok Kumar in post-charge stage.
5. PW-1, PW-3 and PW-4 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 24.06.2009 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity,
expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of three sealed glass bottles of 500 gms each of Vegetable Sauce, dividing it in three parts by taking one sealed bottle as one counterpart, separately sealing and marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.
PW-1/A, Notice as per Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C and Raid Report Ex.
PW-1/C-1.
On the next working day, one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to PA for analysis vide PA Receipt Ex.
PW-1/D and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW-1/E.
PA report Ex. PW- 1/F was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, further investigation was carried out by PW-1.
He sent letter Ex. PW-1/G to M/s National Bakery at its office at 345-47, Joshi Road, Karol Bagh, New Delhi and received the reply Ex. PW-1/G-1 from the accused herein.

The accused sent one label of 'Niraj Vegetable Sauce' claiming that the food article had been purchased by him through a supplier Sh.
Raghuraj.
Further investigation was conducted by PW-2.
He sent letter Ex. PW-2/A to the accused but no reply was received.
He sent letters Ex. PW-2/B and Ex. PW-2/C to the STOs and received their replies.

He also sent letter Ex. PW-2/F to M/s Bhilwara Food Industry at their Trilokpuri In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
2

Office (the manufacturer of Niraj Vegetable Sauce, as per the label furnished by the accused) and received its reply Ex. PW-2/G wherein it denied the sale of its product to the accused and also denied the product in question to be belonging to it.

Various letters Ex. PW-2/E, Ex. PW-2/H, Ex.
PW-2/H-1 and Ex. PW-2/H-2 were sent to various departments to ascertain the constitution of the firms involved.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-2/I was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-2/J was filed in the court.
Intimation Letter Ex. PW-2/K was sent to the accused along with copy of PA report through post vide receipt Ex. PW-2/L.

These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the accused had been falsely implicated or that the sample commodity was not of the same lot or that the intimation letter was not sent at the proper address of the accused or that the manufacturer was intentionally not implicated or that the sample was not taken as per PFA Rules.
6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 21.03.2015 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.

Though accused accepted the proceedings dated 24.06.2009 wherein a sample of vegetable sauce was lifted from him, yet he claimed that the Vegetable Sauce was not for sale but was to be served to the customers alongwith patties, sandwiches etc.
He also claimed that there was label declaration on the glass bottles containing the sample.
He also stated that he did not accept the price of the sample because the sauce was not for public sale.
He took stand that the documents were not read over or explained to him, claiming that his signatures were obtained by FI on several documents.
He questioned the PA report asserting that the sample was conforming to standard and the sample had proper label declaration.
He denied receiving intimation letter and claimed that he was compelled to sign several documents.
Despite given opportunity, accused chose not to lead any evidence in defence.

7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report dated 13.07.2009.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various missing links in the testimony of witnesses.

Ld.
Counsel has contended that the PA report and intimation letter were never received by the accused and thus, the right of the accused under section 13(2) PFA Act stood frustrated.
It is then argued that the food article was not meant for direct sale and therefore, the matter would not be covered under the PFA Act.
It is also submitted that the accused had given representation to the department disclosing the particulars of the manufacturer of the food article who was never implicated in the present case.
Ld. Counsel has also argued that there was defect in the sampling method.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.

10. It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of the PFA Act for the offence of adulteration, as well as Section 2(ix)(k) of In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
3 PFA Act for the offence of misbranding.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.

Section 2(ia)(b)
applies there the article contains any other substance which injuriously affects the nature, substance of quality thereof.
Section 2(ia)(j) specifically deals with colouring matter which is present other than prescribed or is present beyond the prescribed limits of variability.

Section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
Under Section 2(ix)(k) it has to be established that the food article was not labelled in accordance with PFA Act or Rules.
11. The commodity in the present case is stated to be 'Vegetable Sauce', which falls under the main head of 'fruit products'.
There is no dispute about this fact even from the side of the accused, in as much as he never claimed that the food article was something else or other than vegetable sauce.

Though no such stand has been taken by the accused, yet the court needs to ascertain as to how the food article was identified by the FI to be vegetable sauce, particularly when there was no label on the food article giving its description at the time of sampling.

In this regard, Ld. SPP has pointed out that the vendor himself disclosed about identity of the food article as confirmed from the documents Ex. PW-1/A, Ex. PW-1/B, Ex. PW-1/C and Ex. PW-1/C-1 prepared at the spot, all of which mentioned the food article to be vegetable sauce.
In addition to this, it is pertinent to note that the accused never disputed the fact that the sample was of vegetable sauce only.
The accused never gave suggestion to any PW to the effect that the sample was not of vegetable sauce.

Even in his reply Ex.
PW-1/G-1 as given to the FI during investigation, the accused claimed that the sample was of 'Niraj Vegetable Sauce' which is in the nature of an admission of the fact that the sample was of vegetable sauce only.
Even in his statement under Section 313 CrPC, the accused accepted the fact that a sample of 'Vegetable Sauce' was taken from him.

Therefore, throughout the investigation and trial,
the accused accepted the fact that the sample was of vegetable sauce only, and never claimed that it was of some other food article.
12. It is however to be noted that the PA analysed the food article to be a fruit product falling under Item No. A.16.12 of Appendix-B of PFA Rules.
At this stage, it is important to consider that Items No. A.16.01 to A.16.44 of Appendix-B of PFA Rules were substituted by GSR 185(E) dated 21.03.2005.

"Vegetable Sauce" has been a standardized food article, which now falls in Item no.
A.16.28 of the Appendix B of PFA Rules, under the head 'Culinary Pastes / Fruits and Vegetable Sauces other than Tomato Sauce and Soya Sauce' and under the main head "Fruit Products".
Prior thereto, this food article fell under Item No. A.16.12 which pertained to the head 'Sauce' under the larger head 'Fruit Products'.
Detailed standards had been prescribed with respect to 'Sauce' which included fruit and vegetable sauce, as per the Item No. A.16.12, as it existed earlier before the amendment.

As per the standards so prescribed, the total soluble solids should not be less than 15%, total acidity should not be less than 1.0%, the food article should not contain any Coal Tar Dye and it could contain only permitted preservatives.
In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017

Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
4 13.
It is however seen that on the day of sampling, the rules had already been amended and vegetable sauce was now governed by Item No. A.16.28 and fell under clause 2(2) of the said item no..

According to this provision, vegetable sauce should contain total soluble solids not less than 15.0% and the acidity should not be less than 1.2%, food additives as permitted in Appendix-C were allowed but it should not contain any other added colour, whether natural or synthetic.
14.

Apparently, the PA has wrongly mentioned the Item number under which the product "Vegetable Sauce" fell, as Item no. A.16.12 which existed earlier had already been substituted by the new provisions and the food article was now governed by Item No. A.16.28.
Since the PA has not been examined on record, no reason could be ascertained as to why and how he had wrongly mentioned the Item number in his report.
15. However, no benefit can be given to the accused solely on this count.

This is primarily because other than mentioning of wrong Item number, there is no fault or irregularity in the tests conducted and also the standards on which the results have been evaluated by the analysis.

The PA report clearly shows that the food article had been analysed for presence of synthetic colouring matter,
total soluble solids and acidity in terms of acetic acid.
These standards had been mentioned in Item no. A.16.12 (as it existed then) that dealt with the same food article as 'Sauce' and which is now governed by Item No. A.16.28, with slight modification.
The minimum prescribed level of acidity has now been changed to 1.2% instead of earlier existing 1.0%.
Other than this, the standards are the same.
It is therefore not a case where the product was analysed on standards of some other product.
The PA report clearly mentions the prescribed standards of vegetable sauce only.
The sample was not failed with respect to standards of some food article other than "Vegetable Sauce".
It is therefore clear that the PA had wrongly mentioned the Item number under which the food product fell and had applied the standards which had already been amended.

16. In any case, the court is not bound by the Item number mentioned by the PA in its report, as the court is primarily concerned with the results given by the analyst on the basis of chemical analysis.

Since the parameters applied to the food product were correct and as per the prescribed standards,
no benefit can be given to the accused on this count.
The court can still evaluate if the analytical values conformed to the amended standards as prescribed under the rules that existed on the day of sampling.
17. It is pertinent to note that the PA found the presence of the synthetic colouring matters tartrazine, Sunset Yellow FCF and ponceu 4R in violation of Rules 23, 28 and 29 of PFA Rules.
Rule 23 prohibits the addition of colouring matter to any food article except as specifically permitted.
Rule 28 enumerates the synthetic colour that can be used in permitted food articles.

Rule 29 provides the list of food articles where such permitted food article can be used, in the quantities as prescribed in Rule 30.
18.

It would be seen that the food article 'Vegetable Sauce' does not fall in any of the clauses of Rule 29 of PFA Rules, which would mean that no synthetic colour is permitted to be used in this food article.
Even as per Item no. A.16.12 (the old provision) and Item No. A.16.28 (new provision), no such added colour is permissible in preparation of vegetable sauce.

In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
5 19.
Further, Rule 47 of PFA Rules provides that no artificial sweetner shall be added to any food article except in prescribed food articles in permissible limits.
Item no. 1 of Rule 47, pertains to saccharine sodium, which nowhere mentions sauce or vegetable sauce to be a food article where the artificial sweetner saccharine could be used.

The PA found the presence of saccharine in the food article in violation of Rule 47.
20.
In addition to these violations, PA also found the sample to be misbranded because of absence of any label on the food article.

Rule 32 provides that every package of food article should carry a label mentioning in clear, prominent and legible manner the name of the food, list of ingredients,various declarations, its contents and weight, code / batch number, date of manufacture / packing, best before date etc.
The stand of the prosecution is that the food article in question was not having any label as per Rule 32, though this fact has been denied by the accused.
21. The present case is based on the findings of PA as given in report Ex. PW-1/F.
Report of chemical expert is admissible in evidence under section 293 CrPC without formal examination of such expert.

As far as this report is concerned, the contents and findings therein have not been disputed by the defence, though it is claimed that such findings are wrong on account of incorrect sampling methodology.
It is nowhere the defence of the accused that the PA had adopted an incorrect method of analysis or there was some other mistake in the report.

The defence never applied under section 293 CrPC to cross-examine the PA when this option was available to him, so as to question her on the testing methodology adopted by her or to explain other findings in her report.

The report shows that three synthetic colouring matters were found in the sample which were not permitted,
saccharine was found present which was not permitted, total soluble solids were found to be 7.85%
which should have been minimum 15%, total acidity in terms of acetic acid was found to be 0.56%
which should have been minimum 1.0% (as per old rules) or 1.2% (as per new rules).
In the absence of label, the sample was found to be misbranded.
22. The accused has also not exercised his right under section 13(2) PFA Act for getting the sample analysed through CFL.
For this, the arguments are that PA report with intimation letter were never served upon him.

Ld. Defence Counsel has relied upon judgements titled as Rameshwar Dayal v.
State of UP [1996(2) PFA Cases 197], State of Orissa v. Gouranga Sahu [2002 (2) FAC 110] to impress that right under section 13(2) PFA Act is valuable right and it is the duty of the complainant to ensure that such right is not frustrated.

Rameshwar Dayal v.
State of UP [1996(2) PFA Cases 197]

sentences.text: 23. As per the scheme of the Act, after a sample (in three counterparts) is lifted by the FI, he is required as per section 11 to send, by the immediately succeeding working day, one counterpart of sample to PA for analysis and deposit the remaining two counterparts with the LHA.
The PA analyses the sample and delivers report to the LHA under section 13 of Act.

Under section 13(2) of the Act, after institution of prosecution against the accused, the LHA is required to forward a copy of the PA report to the accused, informing that he may apply to the Court, within 10 days of receipt of report, for getting the sample (second counterpart) analysed by CFL.
Thus, this provision mandates sending of PA report to the accused by the LHA.
It is a settled law that if the report is not so sent, it would cause prejudice to the accused and his right cannot be frustrated by the prosecution.

The point to be noted is, that such forwarding of report has to be after the institution of the prosecution In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
6 in the court and not prior to filing of the case.
Also, the accused has 10 days time from the date of receipt of report to apply to the court.

Again, if so applied, the court requires the LHA to produce counterpart of the sample before it, and upon receipt of such requisition, LHA is required to produce it within 5 days (section 13(2-A) of Act) before the court.
The court then sends the said counterpart to the CFL for analyses, and the Director, CFL is required to send report of analysis within 1 month.
24. It is to be noted that sample of vegetable sauce in this case was lifted on 24.06.2009 and it was analysed by PA who gave report dated 13.07.2009.

The complaint was filed on 11.02.2010.
25.
At the outset, there is no merit in the contention that the PA report was not received by the accused.
PW-2 deposed about sending the copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-2/K through registered post vide receipt Ex. PW-2/L.
The evidence also shows that the office file containing documents had been produced in the court at the time of evidence of PW-2 which were seen and returned.
The fact of sending the report was also reaffirmed by PW-3.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the document was not proved, primarily because no objection was raised by the defence at the time when the document was exhibited.
No suggestion was given to any PWs that no such receipt was in existence or that the receipt proved on record was a forged document.
It is not the case where no original receipt exists.
If the accused had any issue about the existence of the original documents, he should have asked the PWs or the complainant department to produce the documents again.
But no such attempt was made by the accused, except putting bald suggestions to the effect that the intimation letter was not sent at proper address or that it was never delivered to him.
It is to be understood that the accused has never disputed the factum of sending the letter through registered post at the trial but has only claimed that it was not sent at a proper address.

Thus, there is no reason for the court to disbelieve the version of PW-2 and PW-3 that the letter was sent to the accused through registered post which did not return undelivered.
26.
Once this fact is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.
The stand taken by the accused, that the letter was not sent at his proper address, has remained bald averment without any evidentiary support.
The accused has not explained what was his 'proper address' if not the one at which the intimation letter was sent.
It would be seen that the intimation letter Ex. PW-2/K was sent at three addresses.
The first address is of handcart at the corner of Allahabad Bank which may not be called as a proper address.

But the second address is of National Bakery at 345-47, Joshi Road, Karol Bagh, which was undoubtedly the correct address of the accused, as gathered from the fact that the letter Ex. PW-1/G was also sent at this address earlier during the course of investigation which was duly replied by the accused himself vide letter Ex.
PW-1/G-1.
It would be clear that the said address was correct and proper address of the accused.

Again, the intimation letter was also sent at the third address of C-33/R-3, T Huts, near Block-K,
Kalibari Marg, New Delhi-110001, which was also a correct and proper address as disclosed by the accused himself in his reply Ex. PW-1/G-1.
This address is appearing even on the photocopy of the I Card of the accused Mark X, the genuineness of which has never been disputed.
The accused was summoned and served at these addresses only and he furnished this address only even in his bail bond.
With such material in hand, there is nothing for the court to conclude that the addresses at which the letter was sent, were not proper addresses.

The accused has also not furnished any other In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
7 address which he claims to be 'proper'.

entities.text: Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: No deficiency in the given addresses has been pointed out by the accused.
There is no merit in such a stand.

In such a position, when a letter had been sent through registered post at correct and proper addresses, there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.

The burden would not upon be the complainant to show delivery of the letter and such burden would now shift upon the accused to show that the letter was not so delivered despite having been sent at correct addresses through registered post.
But the accused has not led any evidence to this effect.
No attempt was made by him to summon the records of postal department to show as to whom the letters were delivered or if they remained undelivered.
There is no evidence to show that the letter was not delivered to the accused.
Accused has not claimed that he was not staying at the given addresses or was staying at some other address or that it could not have been served upon him at the relevant time.
It is not his claim that he was not available at the said addresses or had shifted from those addresses.
Thus, accused has failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
As PW-2 and PW-3 deposed that the registered letter was not received back undelivered, the burden would be upon the accused to prove anything to the contrary.
By not leading any evidence to support his stand, the version of the accused remains unsubstantiated.
Therefore, it has to be held that the intimation letter and PA report were delivered upon the accused in due course.
The accused cannot therefore opt to simply deny the things and claim that PA report was not received by him.
27. Therefore, it cannot be said that the complaint had frustrated his right under section 13(2) PFA Act.
It was upon the accused to have taken steps to send the second counterpart to CFL after service of the intimation letter.
He cannot simply chose to deny the things at the trial without leading any evidence to support such a stand.
28. Similarly, even the time taken by the complainant to file the complaint would not make any difference.

Delay in filing the complaint would be taken in favour of the accused in those cases where the sample sent to CFL is reported to be decomposed, rendering it unfit for analysis, in which case the right of accused can be said to have been frustrated.
If the accused is able to show on concrete grounds that any such delay in filing the prosecution has caused prejudice to him or frustrated his rights, only then the delay can be said to be fatal.
29. In the case at hand, any delay whatsoever would not have made any difference as far as the incriminating ingredient is concerned.

If the delay causes some variation in natural ingredients but the article still fails on account of presence of a prohibited substance, the offence would still be made out, irrespective of such natural changes on account of delay.
The nature, quality and quantity of synthetic colours would not have changed in any manner on account of any time gap, though there might be some changes in natural ingredients.
Even if there was some time gap in filing the complaint, the accused was still having a right under section 13(2) PFA Act and it never stood frustrated.
30. As a corollary, the accused cannot choose to forgo his right to get the sample analysed from CFL under section 13(2) of the Act, citing a particular period of delay.
The accused cannot claim that after lapse of any specific time period, his right would automatically get frustrated or deemed to In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017

Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
8 have been frustrated and would have certainly rendered the sample unfit for analyses.
It is only when the accused exercises such right and the CFL opines that the sample was rendered unfit for analyses that he can get benefit of the delay.

In judgement titled as Britannia New Zealand Foods Pvt. v. Director (PFA) [Crl.MC No. 2069/2008, Delhi High Court, dated 01.06.2012], the Hon'ble High Court was dealing with a matter of 'Cheddar Cheese' which was found not conforming to the standards by the PA.

entities.text: Britannia New Zealand Foods Pvt. v. Director (PFA) [Crl.MC No. 2069/2008
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The complaint was filed after 18 months of procurement of the sample and it had been argued that the sample was a perishable item and had a shelf life of 9 months, after which filing of the complaint had deprived the accused of his right under section 13(2) of the Act.

However,
observing that the accused had not applied under section 13(2) of the Act for analysis of second sample by CFL, it was held that the accused could not claim any benefit on that score.

The Hon'ble court relied upon the precedent titled as Babu Lal Hargovinddas v. State of Gujarat [AIR 1971 SC 1277], where it was held that "There is also in our view no justification for holding that the accused had no opportunity for sending the sample in his custody to the Director, Central Food Laboratory under Section 13(2) because he made no application to the Court for sending it.

entities.text: Babu Lal Hargovinddas v. State of Gujarat [AIR 1971 SC 1277]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It does not avail him at this stage to say that over four months had elapsed from the time the samples were taken to the time when the complaint was filed and consequently the sample had deteriorated and could not be analysed".

The Hon'ble Court also considered that in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ghisa Ram [1967 CriLJ 939] as well, the Director had reported that the sample had become highly decomposed and could not be analysed.

entities.text: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ghisa Ram [1967 CriLJ 939]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If in pursuance of the application the part of the sample was sent to the Director and he had reported that the part of the sample was incapable of analysis for the reason that it was decomposed, the accused could perhaps contend that he was deprived of his right to have the sample analysed by the Director on account of the laches of the complainant and that he should be acquitted.
But, where the accused never applies under Section 13(2) of the Act, he cannot complain that he had been deprived of any right.

It has been categorically laid down that if the accused would have applied to get the sample analysed by the CFL and on analysis, the CFL would have concluded that the sample was decomposed or not fit for analysis, prejudice could be said to have been caused to him as his valuable and statutory right under Section 13(2) of the Act would have been denied to him.
31. Thus, it is clear that the court would not assume that the right of the accused stood frustrated just because of some delay in filing the prosecution.
The right would get frustrated only when he exercises his right under section 13(2) of the Act and the CFL finds the sample to be decomposed or unfit for analysis.
Thus, the matter would depend on case to case basis.

32. In view of this proposition, the accused in this case cannot claim that his right under section 13(2) PFA stood automatically frustrated when the complaint was filed after about seven months of lifting the sample so as to give him an option not to file application to send the sample for analysis to CFL.
Such argument is liable to be rejected.
The judgements relied upon by the accused would therefore not help him in any manner.
33. In the present case, the witnesses have deposed in one voice and have corroborated the version of each other on material particulars.
The fate of the case depends on quality of witnesses and not their quantity or designation or professions.
There is no rule of law that requires the evidence of food officials to be viewed with any suspicion.

What is required is that attempt is made to join public In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
9 persons as witnesses as a matter of prudence.
The court is not oblivious of reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments.
But non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses when they are otherwise truthful and credit worthy and have withstood the test of cross-examination.
No motive has shown to exist giving them reason to depose falsely against the accused.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone, if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.
No such inconsistency can be seen in this case.
No violation of any rule or provision has been pointed out by the defence.
34. PW-1, PW-3 and PW-4 all deposed that they went together at the spot.
All deposed about the steps taken by them in lifting the sample.
No deficiency has been pointed out in such steps, except the defence claiming violation of Rule 22.

It is contended that the FI was required to open the sealed bottles, transfer its contents into a larger container, thoroughly mix the contents evenly and then to divide the same in three parts and pack them separately.
However, I do not find any merit in such a contention, primarily because the bottles were in sealed condition at the time of sampling.
As per 'Note' to Rule 22 of PFA Rules, food sold in packaged condition (sealed container or package) shall be sent for analysis in its original condition, without opening the package.
Therefore, the FI was required by the rules not to open the sealed bottles and any such act of opening the seals would have resulted in violation of Rule 22.
There is no violation of any rule on this count.
35. It is also seen that the presence of food officials at the spot has not been disputed by the accused.
There is no evidence to establish any witness was not present at the spot, as suggested by the accused to PW-3.
Signatures of PW-3 appear on Ex. PW-1/C-1 which was prepared at the spot.
No stand has been taken by the accused in his statement under section 313 CrPC, that any particular witness was not present in the raiding team.
36. Now coming to the defences of the accused.
The accused in his statement under Section 313 CrPC has disputed the correctness of PA report and claimed that the product in question was as per standards.
But there is no evidence on record to establish such a defence of the accused.
No witness has been examined in defence to prove that any such colour was subsequently added by the food officials or any other person in the sealed container.
In the absence of any evidence to this effect, the court cannot assume that the proceedings were not proper or that the PA report is wrong on any ground.
For that matter, no deficiency in PA report has been pointed out during the entire trial.
No suggestion was given to any PW to effect that the sample was not adulterated or misbranded.

Again,
there is no evidence to establish the stand of the accused that he was forced to sign any document or that any document was not read over or explained to him.
No such suggestion was given to the main witness PW- 1 during his cross examination nor any complaint was filed by the accused before any forum in this regard.
Such stands are liable to be rejected.
37. It is then contended that the PA has not given the quantum or percentage or extent of colours or saccharine present so as to determine if they were harmful or not.
It is submitted that such colours and sweetner are permitted for use in certain food articles and are not harmful to human body.

In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
10 38.
However, I do not find myself in agreement with such an argument.
As already discussed, such colours or artificial sweetner are permitted only in specific food articles and vegetable sauce does not find place in those food articles.
Rule 23 prohibits addition of colouring matter in food articles other than those specifically permitted.
Hence, no colour or artificial sweetner could be added to vegetable sauce and use of any such synthetic colour or sweetner is absolutely prohibited.

The obvious inference is that use of such synthetic food colour and sweetner is totally prohibited for use in such vegetable sauce, though they are permitted in specified food articles within the prescribed limits.

Reliance can be safely placed on the precedents titled as Delhi Administration v. Ashwani Kumar [Crl. A. 538/2013, Delhi High Court, Dated 09.05.2013] and Delhi Administration v.
Manohar Lal [Crl. A. 153/2013, Delhi High Court, Dated 18.02.2013] which are squarely applicable to this case as well.
39. Having said so, it is immaterial to go into the question as to what was the percentage or quantity of colours or sweetner used in the sample of vegetable sauce.

sentences.text:
Even if the said quantity was in traces,
as being contended by the Ld. Defence Counsel, that would still make out the offence as these colours and sweetner are not permitted within any limits for use in this food article.
In any case, it would be for the accused to show as to on what basis he claims presence of such colouring matter in traces in food article in question.
The burden would upon be him to show how even traces of colour or sweetner could have entered the food article being sold by him.
But no evidence has been led by the accused to establish this fact.
In this case, no stand has been taken by the accused at the trial that any such colour or sweetner was a result of natural use or the food article exposed to natural environment.
No suggestion to this effect was given to any witness during cross-examination.

No such defence was raised by the accused even in his statement under section 313 CrPC.
40.

All the witnesses have supported the case of each other by deposing in one voice about sample proceedings, about lifting of the sample from the accused, and about the steps in proceedings,
signing of documents etc.
There is no material contradiction in their evidence.

There is nothing in their cross-examination which can be called as contradiction, except the fact that PW-3 deposed that there were 10-12 bottles of sauce in the handcart of the accused but PW-4 claimed that eight bottles were there.
41. It is to be understood that the sample proceedings were conducted in 2009 and the witnesses were cross-examined in 2013, that is, after about four years of the incident.

When evidence was recorded after lapse of such a long period, some contradictions, omissions, additions and improvements are bound to creep in, because human memory is liable to fade with passage of time.
No witness can be expected to remember all minute details of the incident with mathematical accuracy or scientific precision.
Unless some contradiction is material enough to go to the root of the matter, such variations have to be ignored.

42. The said contradiction as appearing in evidence of PW-3 and PW-4 cannot be said to be material enough so as to negate the testimony of the witness on other counts primarily when the sample proceedings have not been disputed by the accused persons.
The accused has admitted the visit of the food officials and lifting of sample from premises.

In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
11 43.
The next defence put forth by the accused is that the food article was not for sale but was only to be served alongwith the other food articles.
Well, the accused has failed to establish such a stand at the trial, primarily because no evidence has been lead by him in defence to substantiate this stand.
In the absence of any evidence, such a version has remained a bald averment.
When no witness has been examined to this extent, even prosecution did not get any opportunity to rebut such a stand or to cross-examine any such witness in this regard.
Mere putting bald suggestions would not be prove any fact in the absence of any positive evidence.

44. In any case, the definition of sale as per section 2(xiii) of PFA Act is quite wide which includes exposing for sale, having in possession for sale, sale for analysis, and also an attempt to sell.

Therefore, when the sample was taken by the Food Inspector against monetary consideration, there was an obvious sale transaction irrespective of the fact if the product had been otherwise sold to any other person on that day or not.
It is also clear that price of the sample was also paid to the accused vide vendor receipt Ex. PW-1/A.
He never claimed at the trial that the price was not accepted by him, as put forth by him for the first time in his statement under Section 313 CrPC which appears to be an afterthought.

If the accused was serving vegetable sauce alongwith the other food articles which were obviously meant for sale for human consumption, such condiment can be said to be a part of the food article itself.
There is nothing to show that the food article was meant for any purpose other than sale under the purview of PFA Act.
Again, section 2 (viiib) of PFA Act (also inserted in 1976 by way of amendment) defines "manufacture" to be including any process incidental or ancillary to the manufacture of an article of food.
45. It is then contended by the accused that the product was actually manufactured by M/s Bhilwara Food Industries, alleging that it has not been implicated intentionally.

In this regard, he has relied upon his reply Ex. PW-1/G-1 sent to the complainant wherein he disclosed that he had purchased the vegetable sauce from one Raghuraj having his factory at 12/17-18, Trilokpuri, Delhi-110091.
He also sent a label of 'Niraj Vegetable Sauce' alongwith his reply, claiming that it was the label of the food article in question.

46. In this regard, it is to be understood that retailers, distributors and manufacturers all operate in their respective fields and all of them can be prosecuted and held liable under Section 7/16 of PFA Act for manufacturing or storing or selling or distributing any such adulterated or misbranded food.
The only benefit which a vendor can claim is under Section 19(2) of PFA Act under the concept of warranty.
Even for that provision to apply, the vendor has to prove that he had a written warranty in the prescribed form and also that the food article was sold by him in the same stage as purchased by him.
Thus, mere bald averment that he had purchased the article from some other person, would not serve any purpose.
47. In the present case, no bill of purchase has been produced by the accused either at the time of sampling or during the investigation or during the trial.

In the absence of any such invoice or bill as per Section 14 of PFA Act read with Rule 12 A of PFA Rules read with Form VIA of PFA Rules, the court is not in a position to guess as to if there was any such bill or warranty and if it was in prescribed format.
In the absence of any warranty in writing, no benefit under Section 19(2) can be given to the accused.

In Re vs Ram Dayal on 4 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16868413/
12 48.
Even otherwise, the stand of the accused is not established appropriately.
As can be seen even by the reply of M/s Bhilwara Food Industry Ex.PW-2/G, the label sent by the accused pertained to a bottle of 400 gm but the bottle as lifted from the accused was of 500 gm.
The accused never chose to summon and examine any person from Bhilwara Food Industry or even Sh. Raghuraj to prove any of his defences.
In the absence of any bill / invoice, it cannot be established if the food article had been purchased by the accused from any particular vendor.
No benefit can be given to the accused on this count.
49. There is no force in the argument that no photograph of the site was taken by the FI at the time of sampling.
There is no mandatory provision to do so.
The corroborative version of the witnesses would be sufficient to implicate the accused.

Similarly, when the accused never disclosed the particulars of the supplier at the time of sampling, there was no occasion for the FI to prepare a notice under Section 14A, as contented by the defence.
50. No other stand has been taken by the accused at the trial or during the course of arguments.

51. The case in hand would be covered under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act as there is evidence to show that the food article was not of the nature, substance or quality which it is "purported" to be as per PFA Rules.

The case would fall under section 2(ia)(j) as there is presence of colours which are not permitted in this article, and under section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act as the constituents of synthetic colours and artificial sweetner was present in quantities not within the prescribed limits, being totally prohibited.

However, in the absence of quantity or percentage of colours or sweetner, it cannot be said that the extent of colours or sweetner used was affecting injuriously its nature,
substance or quality thereof so as to make out violation of section 2(ia)(b).
Similarly, there is clear violation of Rule 32 and Section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act as there was no label on the food article.
Violation of section 2(ia)(j) is punishable under section 16(1A) and violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) as well as Section 2(ix)(k) is punishable under section 16(i)(a) of PFA Act.

But being graver offence, conviction can be under section 16(1A) of PFA Act.
52.
In view of this discussion, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused had sold adulterated and misbranded food in violation of section 2(ia)(a),
(j) and (m) of PFA Act read with Rules 23, 28 and 29 of PFA Rules and also violation of Section 2(ix)(k) read with Rule 32 of PFA Rules, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
53. Having said so, the accused is held guilty and is convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1A) of the PFA Act.
54. Let the matter be listed for arguments on sentence.
